issues.legal_issue: A former trustee must account to the succeeding trustee for the former trustee’s management even when negligence or wilful default is not alleged.
material_facts: The former trustees managed the temple and its properties during their terms of office, and the respondent was the managing trustee.
The succeeding trustees obtained possession of the temple’s properties but had not received accounts of the former trustees’ management.
After a concession before the High Court, the suit was confined to rendition of accounts and payment of any amounts found due, rather than a claim based on negligence or wilful default.
issues.conclusion: The former trustees were liable to render accounts of their management to the succeeding trustees, irrespective of negligence or wilful default.
issues.legal_principle: A trustee is not discharged without rendering accounts of the trustee’s management; that liability is independent of negligence or wilful default. The Court distinguished V. K. Kelu Achan v. C. S. Sivarama Pattar and The Madura Devasthanams v. Doraiswami Nayudu, which did not establish that an ex-trustee need not account absent proof of wilful default.

predicates.accounting_suit_between_successor_and_fo: The succeeding trustee brought a suit seeking accounts from a former trustee.
predicates.former_trustee_managed_trust_property: The former trustee managed property held for the trust.
predicates.management_accounts_not_rendered: The former trustee had not rendered accounts of that management to the succeeding trustee.

issues.definition: When a succeeding trustee sues a former trustee who managed trust property and has not accounted for that management, the former trustee must render those accounts.

issues.legal_issue: The period for which a former trustee must account depends on the circumstances of the case, and an appellate court should not disturb the lower courts’ discretionary selection without justification.
material_facts: The trial court directed accounts from the beginning of 1946 until the succeeding trustees took possession of the temple in July 1952.
The first appellate court upheld that period after considering the circumstances of the case.
The Supreme Court found no justification to interfere with the lower courts’ exercise of discretion.
issues.conclusion: The period for which accounts were required depended on the facts of the case, and the lower courts’ selected period was not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: There is no fixed limit for an account against a trustee; the period is determined in the court’s discretion in light of the circumstances, including the considerations discussed in Attorney General v. Exeter Mayor. The Court also referred to Sanyasayya v. Murthamma and Hariharabrahmam v. Janakiramiah as examples of case-specific periods for accounting.

predicates.appeal_challenges_discretionary_accounti: A party appealed a lower-court decision fixing the period for which a trustee must account.
predicates.lower_courts_selected_period_after_consi: The lower courts selected the accounting period after considering the circumstances of the case.
predicates.no_justification_to_interfere_is_shown: The appeal disclosed no justification for interfering with the lower courts’ selection.

issues.definition: On an appeal challenging an accounting period selected by the lower courts in light of the case circumstances, the period remains undisturbed when no justification for interference is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on suits concerning religious-institution administration or management does not bar a general-law suit for accounts from a former trustee when the statute makes no provision for determining that dispute.
material_facts: The succeeding trustees brought a civil suit against a former trustee for accounts of the former trustee’s management.
The applicable statutory provision restricted suits concerning administration or management, and other disputes for whose determination the statute made provision.

The statutory chapter on budgets, accounts and audit addressed financial supervision, audits, and surcharge procedures, but did not provide for deciding a succeeding trustee’s claim for accounts from a former trustee.
The claim for accounts did not fall within a statutory procedure that determined that dispute.
issues.conclusion: The statutory provision did not bar the suit for accounts, and the suit was maintainable in the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil courts have jurisdiction over civil suits unless their jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred. Section 93 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 restricts suits only in matters for which the Act makes provision; Chapter VII, including sections 70–74, did not provide for determining an ex-trustee’s liability to account to a present trustee. The Court relied on the construction of section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Appanna v. Narasinga and Tirumalai Tirupati Devasthanam Committee v. Udiavar Krishnayya Sahnbhaga, and the interpretation of the corresponding earlier statutory wording in Manjeshwar Srimad Anantheswar Temple v. Vaikunta Bhakta. It distinguished Venkataratnam v. Narasimha Rao and considered Sri Sarveswaraswami Vari Temple v. Rudrapaka Veerabhadrayya in explaining the scope of the statutory bar.

predicates.civil_suit_seeks_accounts_from_former_tr: A party brought a civil suit seeking accounts from a former trustee for that trustee’s management.
predicates.statutory_procedure_does_not_resolve_for: The applicable statutory procedures do not provide for determining the dispute over the former trustee’s accounts to the succeeding trustee.

issues.definition: A civil suit seeking accounts from a former trustee remains within civil-court jurisdiction when the applicable statutory procedures do not resolve that accounting dispute.
